title: LearnLens: LLM-Enabled Personalised, Curriculum-Grounded Feedback with Educators in the Loop
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing timely, high-quality, personalised feedback to students while reducing teacher workload. The authors argue that existing LLM-based assessment and feedback tools often focus too narrowly on scoring, lack sufficient curricular grounding, and provide limited opportunities for educator oversight or revision. The paper introduces LearnLens as a response to these shortcomings, aiming to support both scalable feedback generation and meaningful teacher control in science education.

LearnLens is a modular LLM-based system with separate teacher-facing and student-facing interfaces. Its core components include an error-aware assessment module that awards partial credit based on concept-level alignment to curriculum-linked mark schemes, a curriculum-grounded retrieval and generation approach called a Chain-of-Concept framework that organises prior assessments by topic rather than only similarity, and an educator-in-the-loop workflow that allows teachers to inspect, revise, and propagate edits to AI-generated feedback. The system also includes verifier models that rate feedback for scientific accuracy, clarity, and specificity, and iteratively improve outputs when scores fall below a threshold.

The empirical evaluation is situated in GCSE science, indicating a high-school context, and involved 30 participants with prior STEM teaching experience at either high school or college level who interacted with the system and completed a structured questionnaire. In addition, the system’s scoring and efficiency were tested on 100 authentic student answers to a five-mark short-essay science question. All experiments were locally deployed because of student data privacy concerns. The paper is focused on teacher perceptions and system performance rather than direct measurement of student learning gains, and it explicitly notes that student evaluation is still lacking.

The main conclusions are that LearnLens was positively received by teacher participants, with high ratings for usability, responsiveness, relevance to instructional goals, and scientific accuracy. Compared with direct-prompt baselines using the same underlying foundation models, the modular LearnLens pipeline achieved better scoring quality with competitive latency and cost. The authors conclude that LearnLens shows promise as a practical classroom-ready AI feedback assistant that can reduce grading workload and support more targeted guidance, while acknowledging the need for future evaluation with students.

identified_tools.name: LearnLens
identified_tools.description: A modular LLM-based educational feedback system for science education that provides personalised, curriculum-grounded assessment and feedback with teacher oversight through educator- and student-facing interfaces.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a science feedback tool that generates curriculum-aligned mark schemes, scores short-answer responses with error-aware assessment, produces personalised feedback, supports teacher review/revision, and provides performance visualisation and verifier scores.

findings.finding_summary: In a user study with 30 participants who had prior STEM teaching experience, LearnLens received consistently positive usability and performance ratings: across nine Likert-scale items, the mean rating never fell below 4.1/5. About 80% of teachers described the menu structure as intuitive, and 75% expected results in under 15 seconds; the paper states LearnLens met this threshold in more than 90% of cases during local deployment.
findings.measure: Teacher questionnaire ratings on usability, responsiveness, and interface intuitiveness
findings.effect_size: mean ratings >=4.1/5; 80% intuitive; 75% acceptable wait time under 15s; >90% met threshold

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported time savings relative to prior practice. Q12 indicated that half of teachers previously spent 10–30 minutes per assignment, whereas the median time with LearnLens fell below 5 minutes; additionally, 26 of 30 respondents ranked speed as the tool's top strength.
findings.measure: Self-reported teacher time per assignment and perceived speed advantage
findings.effect_size: 50% previously spent 10–30 min; median with LearnLens <5 min; 26/30 ranked speed top strength

findings.finding_summary: Adoption intent was positive across prior-workflow groups, with no significant difference by prior method. A chi-square test found no significant group difference in overall adoption intent (p=0.63), and every cohort exceeded 65% on 'continue using,' with the automation-savvy group peaking at 85%.
findings.measure: Teacher adoption intent / future preference for using the tool
findings.effect_size: p=0.63; all groups >65% continue using; peak 85%

findings.finding_summary: On 100 authentic student answers to a five-mark short-essay science question, LearnLens achieved the best scoring quality among compared systems. It reported MSE=3.190, Pearson correlation=0.388, exact accuracy=0.354, and ±1 accuracy=0.747, outperforming the best baseline values reported in the table.
findings.measure: Automated scoring quality on science short-essay responses (MSE, Pearson correlation, exact-match accuracy, within-one-mark accuracy)

findings.finding_summary: LearnLens achieved stronger efficiency than the largest reasoning baseline while maintaining strong performance. Average generation latency was 11.39s (min 7.59s, max 16.97s) with per-request cost $0.0099, described as comparable to Qwen2.5-32B and four times faster and 72% cheaper than QwQ-32B.
findings.effect_size: Avg.=11.39s; Min.=7.59s; Max.=16.97s; Cost=$0.0099; 4x faster and 72% cheaper than QwQ-32B

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's LLaMA family of large language models, used here as a baseline foundation model for direct-prompt scoring, feedback generation, and verification.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a baseline model without the LearnLens modular pipeline, performing scoring, feedback generation, and verification through direct prompting on science student answers.

findings.finding_summary: As a baseline on 100 authentic student answers to a five-mark short-essay science question, LLaMA reported weaker scoring quality than LearnLens: MSE=3.468, correlation=0.235, exact accuracy=0.190, and ±1 accuracy=0.646. It was the fastest and cheapest baseline in the table, with average latency 5.14s and cost $0.0040 per request.
findings.measure: Automated scoring quality plus latency/cost on science short-essay responses

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba's Qwen family of large language models, used here as baseline foundation models for direct-prompt scoring, feedback generation, and verification.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as baseline models without the LearnLens modular architecture, directly prompted to score and generate feedback/verification for science student answers.

findings.finding_summary: Qwen baselines were evaluated on 100 authentic student answers to a five-mark short-essay science question. Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct achieved MSE=3.658, correlation=0.230, exact accuracy=0.241, and ±1 accuracy=0.633 with 12.39s average latency and $0.0096 cost; QwQ-32B achieved MSE=3.506, correlation=0.323, exact accuracy=0.329, and ±1 accuracy=0.709 with 45.49s average latency and $0.0351 cost.
findings.measure: Automated scoring quality plus latency/cost on science short-essay responses

quality_tier_rationale: The paper reports an empirical system evaluation with a teacher user study and benchmark-style performance comparison, but it does not present an RCT or quasi-experimental design measuring student learning outcomes. Evidence is therefore promising but primarily usability/performance-oriented rather than causal effectiveness evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported results are positive for teacher usability, time savings, and automated scoring quality, but the paper does not provide standardized student outcome effect sizes or causal learning gains. Impact appears promising yet remains unclear for student learning.
